issues.legal_issue: The constitutional meaning of agricultural income follows the income-tax definition in force when that definition is applied, rather than being fixed by the definition in force when the Constitution commenced.
material_facts: The taxpayer argued that the constitutional term agricultural income was confined to the definition in the 1922 income-tax legislation, which was in force when the Constitution commenced.
The constitutional text referred to agricultural income as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to income tax, using a general reference to enactments in the plural.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional meaning of agricultural income is the meaning given to it by the income-tax enactment in force at the relevant time.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 366(1), a general reference to the law governing a subject adopts that law as it stands when applied, including subsequent amendments consistent with the purpose of the reference. The Court applied the general-reference principle stated in Bajaya v. Gopikabai & Anr.

predicates.constitutional_meaning_of_tax_term_dispu: A dispute concerns the constitutional meaning of a tax-related term.
predicates.constitution_refers_generally_to_income_: The constitutional text refers generally to income-tax enactments rather than identifying a specific enactment or a fixed version of one.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the constitutional meaning of a tax-related term and the Constitution refers generally to income-tax enactments, the term takes the meaning given by the income-tax law in force when applied.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament may define agricultural income for the purposes of income-tax legislation, while the States may tax agricultural income and the Union may tax other income.
material_facts: The taxpayer challenged the validity of amendments that excluded specified agricultural land in or near urban areas from the exclusion for agricultural land in the definition of capital asset and treated income from its transfer as outside agricultural income.
The constitutional division of taxing authority assigns taxes on agricultural income to the States and taxes on income other than agricultural income to the Union.
issues.conclusion: The amendments defining the relevant land and transfer income as outside agricultural income were within Parliament’s authority and were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(1), Entry 46 of List II and Entry 82 of List I together permit Parliament to define agricultural income for the purposes of the current income-tax enactment; the States may legislate on taxes on agricultural income, and the Union may legislate on other income. The Court relied on The Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. v. State of Kerala & Ors. for this allocation of authority and on the general-reference principle in Bajaya v. Gopikabai & Anr.

predicates.constitutional_taxing_power_dispute: A dispute concerns which level of government may define or tax a category of income under the constitutional allocation of taxing powers.
predicates.constitutional_agricultural_income_defin: The constitutional meaning of agricultural income follows the income-tax law in force when applied.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the constitutional allocation of taxing powers and the constitutional definition follows current income-tax law, Parliament may define agricultural income for income-tax purposes.

issues.legal_issue: Gain from transferring agricultural land that falls within the statutory urban-area criteria is chargeable as capital gains rather than exempt as agricultural income.
material_facts: The taxpayer sold agricultural land situated within municipal limits and realized gains from the sales.

The income-tax legislation excluded specified agricultural land within qualifying municipal areas, and land within that exclusion was not treated as agricultural land for the relevant capital-asset definition.
An explanation to the definition of agricultural income provided that income from transferring such land was not agricultural income; the tax authorities assessed the gains as capital gains.
issues.conclusion: The gains from the sales were liable to capital gains tax, and the High Court was right to reject the taxpayer’s challenge and answer the reference against him.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1A), 2(14)(iii) and 45 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as amended, income from transferring agricultural land within the specified urban-area criteria falls outside agricultural income and is chargeable as capital gains. The Court held that Parliament could make the relevant amendments under the constitutional division of taxing authority, applying Article 366(1), Entries 46 and 82, and The Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. v. State of Kerala & Ors.; it also applied the general-reference principle stated in Bajaya v. Gopikabai & Anr.

rule.if: capital_gains_tax_challenge_or_reference and land_is_agricultural and land_within_qualifying_urban_area and transfer_income_is_excluded_from_agricultural_income

predicates.capital_gains_tax_challenge_or_reference: A taxpayer challenges or a court considers in a tax reference whether gain from a land transfer is chargeable as capital gains.
predicates.land_is_agricultural: The land transferred is agricultural land.
predicates.land_within_qualifying_urban_area: The agricultural land is within an urban area meeting the applicable statutory criteria.
predicates.transfer_income_is_excluded_from_agricul: The applicable income-tax definition excludes income from transferring that land from agricultural income.

issues.definition: If a capital-gains tax challenge or reference concerns agricultural land within a qualifying urban area and the applicable definition excludes its transfer income from agricultural income, the gain is chargeable as capital gains.
